Theme: Medication as Distributed Family Work
Theme definition: Older adults take their own medicine and know it by strip, colour, place, and meal, not by name. The names, the paper, the buying, and the doctor's words sit with a son, daughter, or spouse, and they call this sensible rather than a loss. Reminding belongs to whoever is present, a family question settles a doubt, and being checked is received as care with one limit: not to be watched all the time. Friends' talk is heard; only the doctor changes a medicine. A few manage entirely alone.
Sub-theme: Retained Autonomy in Taking, Delegated Knowledge to Kin
What it means: Swallowing the tablet is the older adult's own act and nobody hands it to them. The long names, the prescription, the pharmacy trip, and what the doctor said are handed to a child or spouse, and this is described as sensible and easing, not as dependence.
Consequence (leads to next theme): This arrangement works by presence and habit. When the routine breaks or nobody is near, the dose is lost and, as the next theme shows, no tool or paper the older adult can use catches it.

Theme: Routine Breakdown and the Inaccessibility of Existing Aids
Theme definition: Doses slip when guests, work, or travel change the day, and the miss is caught only if someone is near; when the family is busy or away nobody asks. The tools offered so far do not reach them: a phone alarm set by a child rings without saying why and is abandoned, an app is too many steps, a button phone has two keys they know. Prescriptions are small print and handwriting the pharmacy reads for them; a new packet is not recognised; a strip runs out and they cannot go to buy. The frustration is dependence at exactly the moments nobody is there.
Sub-theme: Time Slipping Outside the Home Routine
What it means: Nobody describes forgetting as a failing mind. At home, with the strip in front of them and the family around, the routine carries itself; away from it, in talk, travel, or work without fixed hours, the time goes. On trips the medicine itself is left behind.
Consequence (leads to next theme): Each of these barriers names what a phone would have to do instead: speak, show, ring again, reach them outside, read the paper, and watch the stock. The next theme carries those wants.

Theme: Design Expectations for an Accessible Medication Reminder
Theme definition: The technology older adults describe is concrete. It speaks the medicine time in plain Bangla, simply and not loudly in company, because they will not read a screen. It shows a picture of the tablet, marks morning and night with sun and moon, and says which medicine is new. It rings again if they do not respond, reminds them to carry the medicine before going out, and works in the field or at a relative's house. It reads the handwritten paper and tells the buyer before the strip finishes, if it is correct. The older adult presses one big button and nothing more; the child sets it up.
Sub-theme: Spoken Bangla Reminders with Privacy in Company
What it means: Voice is preferred almost unanimously: they do not look at the phone, cannot read small print, and glasses are not always at hand. The voice must be simple, respectful, in Bangla, and private when others are around.
Consequence (leads to next theme): A phone that does all this still has to find its place among the people who already remind, check, buy, and decide. The last theme is where the older adults put it.

Theme: Negotiating the Agent's Place in the Care Network
Theme definition: Older adults place the phone inside the arrangement they already have, not above it. It reminds where nobody is, in the field or at a relative's house, while at home the wife knows what the phone cannot, so they want both. It may tell one child when a dose is really missed, after time is given, but never watch every dose, and a forgotten press must not be counted as a missed dose. It is trusted because the son put it in and because people they know use it. It gives small information and defers to the doctor; it never decides, and family is family.
Sub-theme: The Agent Where Family Is Absent, Family Where It Is Present
What it means: The phone's place is where family is absent. At home the spouse knows whether they have eaten and is preferred, but she is sometimes busy, so the phone and the family together are better than either alone.
Consequence (leads to next theme): This closes the older adults' account and fixes the prototype's terms: voice to the older adult, a picture and a button, configuration and stock alerts to the child, escalation only on a real miss with time allowed, the record below the act, information without decision, and the family kept in. Phase 2 tests whether the deployed agent kept to them.
